sources.title: Anagarika Dharmapala (Q3518574), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-23): English label 'Anagarika Dharmapala', description 'Sri Lankan Buddhist revivalist and writer (1864-1933)', Sinhala label අනගාරික ධර්මපාල, no Korean label, born 17 September 1864, died 29 April 1933, instance of human. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

George D. Bond, 'Anagarika Dharmapala', Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference/Gale; read in full on Encyclopedia.com, with its bibliography of Bond, Gombrich and Obeyesekere). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: the leading figure in the Sri Lankan Buddhist renaissance of the late colonial period; born Don David Hewavitarana into an elite Sinhala Buddhist family, joined Olcott and Blavatsky's Theosophical circle in 1884, made himself an anagarika (homeless one) who was neither monk nor layman, founded the Maha Bodhi Society to restore the Bodh Gaya shrine, critiqued colonial and Christian suppression of Buddhism through writing and oratory, linked Buddhism to Sinhala nationalism, popularised a lay-oriented reformed Buddhism, and represented Buddhism at the 1893 World Parliament of Religions in Chicago. Short scholarly reference entry; admiring in outline but names the nationalism.

'Dharmapala, Anagarika', World Religions Reference Library (Gale; student-level profile, read in full on Encyclopedia.com). Popular reference biography: birth in Colombo on 17 September 1864, Christian mission schools, work for Olcott, change of name to Dharmapala and the yellow robe, Maha Bodhi Society and journal, the 1893 Chicago Parliament, American patron Mary Foster, the Sinhala Bauddhaya (1906), British Buddhist Mission (1926), ordination in January 1933 and death at Sarnath. Contains over-statements (that he introduced Buddhism to the United States and Europe, that he founded the Society at Blavatsky's side) which are not repeated; used only for outline facts confirmed by the other sources.

Bhadrajee Hewage, 'Anagarika Dharmapala (1864-1933)', St Andrews Encyclopaedia of Theology (University of St Andrews, published 7 August 2025; read in full). Scholarly entry built on Kemper, Obeyesekere, Roberts and Dharmapala's diaries: his family and the 1886 break with lay life, the brahmacharya vow, the yellow robe taken in October 1895, ordination in 1931-33, his lack of any clerical mentor, wide reading, the Gihivinaya lay code (1898), the failed Ethico-Psychological College (1898) and the Kandy novice seminary (1925), dependence on the Hawaiian patron Mary Foster ($50,000 in 1919, $100,000 in 1923), the failure of the Bodh Gaya campaign by 1906. States plainly that his legacy is contested between an icon who bridged the colonised present and the Buddhist past and a nativist whose rhetoric demonised minorities, and that he distanced himself from party politics.

K. T. S. Sarao, 'The Politics of Anagarika Dharmapala and Its Aftermath', chapter in The History of Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya (Springer, Singapore, 2020; text read in full). COUNTER-VOICE: critical scholarly account of his Bodh Gaya campaign, citing Kinnard, Kemper, Trevithick and the 1895 Calcutta High Court judgment: the Maha Bodhi Society founded 31 May 1891 and moved to Calcutta in 1892; the failed attempt to buy out the mahant; the 25 February 1895 installation of a Japanese Buddha image and the ensuing suit; his rejection of advice from Prince Damrong (1892) and Sri Lankan supporters; the court finding that Buddhists had a right of worship but that he had taken the law into his own hands; his anti-Hindu rhetoric; the wariness of Thai, Burmese and other Buddhist leaders; and his part in the Tamil dalit Buddhist movement with Iyothee Thass. Strongly critical in tone; the rhetoric is quoted from other scholars and is not scored as a trait.

Sandagomi Coperahewa (ed.), 'Anagarika Dharmapala and India-Sri Lanka Relations: 150th Birth Anniversary Commemorative Volume 1864-2014' (Centre for Contemporary Indian Studies, University of Colombo, 2015; PDF read). Commemorative university volume with essays by Guruge, Disanayaka, Surendran, Tilakaratne and others, a review of Kemper's biography, the Maha Bodhi Society's history, and 'The Life and Work of Anagarika Dharmapala', a chronology from the Maha Bodhi Journal (1927) extended to his death: the January 1886 departure from government service, the vow at Bodh Gaya on 2 January 1891, the 1891 founding, the January 1892 journal, the first organised pilgrimage of December 1894, the February 1895 image and case, the 1910 Burmese Rest House defeat, the quarrel with Olcott in 1904, internment in Calcutta from June 1915 to 1920, the Calcutta Vihara (1915-20), Sarnath Vihara (1922-30), British Buddhist Mission (1926) and ordination (1931 and 16 January 1933). Society-side and admiring, with a source-critical review inside.

John Henry Barrows (ed.), 'The World's Parliament of Religions: an illustrated and popular story of the World's first Parliament of Religions, held in Chicago in connection with the Columbian Exposition of 1893', vol. 2 (Chicago: Parliament Publishing Company, 1893; Internet Archive scan, University of Toronto copy; OCR text read for all passages naming him). Contemporary record by the Parliament's chairman: reprints the letter of the High Priest of the Southern Buddhist Church of Ceylon presenting 'our young lay-missionary, H. Dharmapala', his addresses 'The World's Debt to Buddha' and 'Buddhism and Christianity', an eyewitness report that the Buddhists were 'surrounded by curious and eager auditors', and Barrows's own account of the day Dharmapala asked a large audience how many had read the life of Buddha, received five answers and said 'How dare you judge us', which Barrows thought 'not altogether fair'. Carries the captioned portrait plate used for the portrait. Partly his own speech; the surrounding comment is by a Christian organiser.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_dharmapala_ccis, src_dharmapala_saet, src_dharmapala_sarao, src_dharmapala_wrrl | 1886-1930 | university commemorative volume, scholarly encyclopaedia, critical scholarly chapter, popular reference] He left government service in 1886 to work for Buddhist schools and press, vowed at Bodh Gaya in January 1891 to rescue the temple, founded the Maha Bodhi Society on 31 May 1891 and its journal in January 1892, started the Buddhagaya Fund (1894), bought land at Sarnath (1901), opened an industrial school there (1904), began the Sinhala Bauddhaya (1906) and a free hospital (1914), and established the British Buddhist Mission (1926). The chronology is the Society's own, but the scholarly and critical sources confirm the founding, the journal and the missions. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 82 / 0.66 to 78 / 0.62 because the hospital, the industrial school and the mission are documented mainly in the Society's own chronology; the founding of the Society and journal is confirmed independently. Lead review lowered this row from 78 / 0.62 to 74 / 0.58 because the chronology of his institutions is the Society's own account, so the breadth of initiatives is partly institutional self-report.

persistence.rationale: [src_dharmapala_ccis, src_dharmapala_saet, src_dharmapala_sarao | 1891-1930 | university commemorative volume, scholarly encyclopaedia, critical scholarly chapter] He pursued the Bodh Gaya campaign from 1891 through a court defeat in 1895 and a final legal loss in 1906, built a Vihara in Calcutta from 1915 to 1920 while restricted to India after the 1915 riots, and laid the Sarnath Vihara foundation in 1922 and completed it in 1930, ordaining only in 1931-33. The same sources record that the campaign fizzled, the 1898 college failed and many of his monk pupils left, so persistence is shown more than success. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 78 / 0.6 to 74 / 0.56 because the Calcutta and Sarnath building and the 1915 restriction come from the Society's own chronology, while the independent scholarly sources stress that the campaign itself fizzled.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_dharmapala_sarao, src_dharmapala_ccis, src_dharmapala_barrows, src_dharmapala_saet | 1891-1906 | critical scholarly chapter, university commemorative volume, 1893 conference record, scholarly encyclopaedia] He publicly challenged the Bodh Gaya mahant, installed a Japanese Buddha image against him in February 1895 and sued after the mahant's men removed it, against the advice of his own Sri Lankan supporters (Sarao); at a side meeting of the 1893 Parliament, when only five in a large audience had read the life of the Buddha, he said 'How dare you judge us' (Barrows, who thought it unfair); the Society's chronology records a breach with Olcott in 1904 and a campaign against the Theosophical Society in 1906. Several sources also record sharp polemics against other religions, and Thai, Burmese and Sri Lankan allies drew back, so impact is dual-edged. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 78 / 0.6 to 76 / 0.58 because the Olcott and Theosophical Society quarrels are told only in the Society's chronology and the 1895 episode is selected by a strongly critical chapter (the court judgment it cites is independent).

leadership_drive.rationale: [src_dharmapala_ccis, src_dharmapala_barrows, src_dharmapala_sarao, src_dharmapala_saet | 1886-1926 | university commemorative volume, 1893 conference record, critical scholarly chapter, scholarly encyclopaedia] He was general secretary of the Buddhist Section and then of the Maha Bodhi Society, sent four monks to Bodh Gaya in July 1891 and organised the first group pilgrimage of Sri Lankan Buddhists there in December 1894; the 1893 Parliament record lists him as general secretary and the letter of the High Priest of the Southern Buddhist Church of Ceylon calls him its young lay missionary. Sarao (citing Kemper) adds that his imperious manner and self-appointed claim to speak for 475 million Buddhists made other Buddhist leaders wary. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 76 / 0.6 to 72 / 0.56 because the office-holding and the pilgrimage rest on the Society's own chronology, and the critical chapter shows other Buddhist leaders did not accept his lead.

persuasiveness.rationale: [src_dharmapala_barrows, src_dharmapala_saet, src_dharmapala_ebuddhism, src_dharmapala_ccis | 1891-1904 | 1893 conference record, scholarly encyclopaedia, reference encyclopaedia, university commemorative volume] Barrows's 1893 record quotes an eyewitness that the Buddhists, represented by Hirai and Dharmapala, were surrounded by curious and eager auditors; the Maha Bodhi Society's chronology and the scholarly entry show that Burmese, Japanese, Thai and Hawaiian supporters (above all Mary Foster, whom he met in October 1893) gave money, a branch society and a Buddha image. The reference entry calls his oratory brilliant; most evidence is of supporters won over rather than a documented act of persuasion in his own words. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.54 strong inference to 64 / 0.46 inference because the evidence is mostly outcomes (donors, delegations) and praise rather than a documented act of persuading named people, and the one contemporary eyewitness line is about audience curiosity.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_dharmapala_saet, src_dharmapala_ccis, src_dharmapala_ebuddhism, src_dharmapala_wrrl | 1886-1933 | scholarly encyclopaedia, university commemorative volume, reference encyclopaedia, popular reference] Passed over for the family business by his father, he left government service in January 1886 and the family home in November 1886 to work for the welfare of Buddhism, and the Society ran rural schools, a free hospital (1914), an industrial school at Sarnath and a sangha seminary. The scholarly source frames his aim as Buddhist and Sinhala welfare specifically, and the critical chapter shows the same campaigns pressing a Buddhist claim against Hindus, so the evidence for serving a wider public good is partial. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 74 / 0.56 to 68 / 0.5 because his stated purpose is read largely from his own diaries and the Society's account, and the same campaigns were framed as a Buddhist, partly Sinhala, claim.

autonomy_need.rationale: [src_dharmapala_saet, src_dharmapala_sarao, src_dharmapala_ebuddhism | 1886-1931 | scholarly encyclopaedia, critical scholarly chapter, reference encyclopaedia] He sought no clerical teacher in Ceylon, created for himself the status of anagarika between layman and monk for about thirty years, delayed ordination until 1931, and made the Maha Bodhi Society the centre of access to Bodh Gaya, which made other Buddhist leaders wary (Sarao, citing Kemper). The Tilakaratne review quoted in the commemorative volume warns that his diaries are also shaped for readers, so the inner motive is not scored. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 72 / 0.52 strong inference to 68 / 0.48 inference because the account of his independence and the wariness of other leaders traces to one scholarly base (Kemper, read by both Hewage and Sarao) and his own diaries.

risk_tolerance.rationale: [src_dharmapala_sarao, src_dharmapala_ccis | 1892-1895 | critical scholarly chapter, university commemorative volume] After failing to buy out the mahant he installed the Japanese image in February 1895 and went to the Calcutta High Court, ignoring the telegrams of Sri Lankan supporters and Prince Damrong's 1892 advice to work in harmony with the Hindus (Sarao); the Calcutta court held that he had taken the law into his own hands even though Buddhists gained a right of worship. Financial and legal exposure is documented, but the sources do not show how he weighed it.

adaptability.rationale: [src_dharmapala_saet, src_dharmapala_ccis, src_dharmapala_sarao | 1886-1925 | scholarly encyclopaedia, university commemorative volume, critical scholarly chapter] He moved from white-robed Theosophical Buddhist worker to the yellow-robed anagarika in October 1895 just after the legal defeat, quarrelled with Olcott in 1904 and campaigned against the Theosophical Society in 1906 (although Kemper, reviewed in the commemorative volume, finds he stayed loyal to theosophy to his death), shifted from the temple campaign to schools, a press and a seminary, and resumed building after his 1915 internment. These shifts are documented, but the critical chapter notes he also kept pressing the same Bodh Gaya aim. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): evidence type lowered from strong inference to inference (score and confidence unchanged at 62 / 0.46) because each of the shifts rests on a single source and the confidence is below the strong-inference band.

discipline.rationale: [src_dharmapala_saet, src_dharmapala_wrrl, src_dharmapala_barrows | 1886-1933 | scholarly encyclopaedia, popular reference, 1893 conference record] He took the brahmacharya vow in 1886 (celibacy, a vegetarian diet, ochre robes, regular meditation and reading) and held to the renunciant life for nearly fifty years until ordination in 1931 and higher ordination in January 1933; Barrows in 1893 already calls him a gentle ascetic. The vow is mainly described from his own diaries as read by Kemper and Hewage, and the Tilakaratne review in the commemorative volume notes that Kemper's reading of those diaries also shows his own recorded sexual feelings and troubled associations with women, so the evidence is of a long, imperfectly kept vow. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.5 strong inference to 62 / 0.44 inference because the vow and the way of life are described from his own diaries and robes, and the commemorative volume's reviewer notes the same diaries record his struggles with it.

curiosity.rationale: [src_dharmapala_saet | 1884-1930 | scholarly encyclopaedia] Hewage, citing Kemper, records that he read widely in religion, science and the occult, that the books named in his diaries run to roughly seventy single-spaced pages, and that he carried an annotated Bible; it is one source family and a general description. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.44 to 58 / 0.4 because it rests on one sentence of one scholarly entry.

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_dharmapala_ccis, src_dharmapala_saet, src_dharmapala_sarao | 1891-1930 | university commemorative volume, scholarly encyclopaedia, critical scholarly chapter] The Society's chronology says that for nearly twenty years it received little help; he raised money from Burmese, Sri Lankan, Japanese and Hawaiian donors (Foster gave $50,000 in 1919 and $100,000 in 1923), secured a share of Buddha relics from the Government of India in exchange for a Calcutta Vihara, and kept a press and schools running. Mostly donor-dependent rather than improvised, so only a modest score. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.44 to 58 / 0.4 because most funding came from a few donors, above all one patron, rather than from improvised means.

collaboration.rationale: [src_dharmapala_sarao, src_dharmapala_ccis, src_dharmapala_saet | 1891-1906 | critical scholarly chapter, university commemorative volume, scholarly encyclopaedia] He worked with Olcott and Blavatsky, the Tamil reformer Iyothee Thass (the Dravida Mahajana Sabha, 1891), Mary Foster, Burmese and Japanese Buddhists and Bengali hosts, but fell out with Olcott and the Theosophical Society, the Burmese members and the Thai court, and Sarao (citing Kemper) says his imperious manner made other Buddhist leaders wary. Mixed evidence, so the score sits near the middle.

portrait.source: Halftone plate of a photograph of Dharmapala (aged 29, photographer not named) captioned 'H. DHARMAPALA, CEYLON.' under a quotation from his Parliament address, placed before page 861 in John Henry Barrows (ed.), The World's Parliament of Religions, vol. 2 (Chicago: Parliament Publishing Company, 1893); the volume's list of illustrations also names 'H. Dharmapala, Ceylon'. Internet Archive scan of the University of Toronto (Robarts) copy, item worldsparliament02barruoft, leaf 65 of the PDF. The photograph was cropped from the page scan (margins, caption and the printed copyright notice in the lower-left corner removed) and downscaled to 714 x 1000; the page scan is 2522 x 4152, so nothing is upscaled.
portrait.license: Public domain by age: published in the United States in 1893 (before 1931); the photographer is not named and the Internet Archive record marks the book NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT.
portrait.attribution: Photographer not named; plate 'H. Dharmapala, Ceylon', in J. H. Barrows (ed.), The World's Parliament of Religions, vol. 2, Chicago: Parliament Publishing Co., 1893 (Internet Archive scan, University of Toronto; cropped and downscaled).
portrait.creator: Unnamed photographer (reproduced in Barrows's Parliament of Religions, Chicago)

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: RISKY (Stage B) / REPLACED. The lead (Library of Congress Bain News Service glass negative ggbain 38893 'A. Hewarritaina Dharmapala', Commons file 'A. Hewarritaina Dharmapala LCCN2014719032.jpg') did not survive: the Bain title is 'unverified data provided by the Bain News Service', Commons gives 1926 while its structured data says 1900, an embedded Time snippet describes a man of 77 although Dharmapala would have been about 61 in 1926, and the LOC item page returns 403 to automated clients (recorded as a bot wall, not bypassed; the LOC general legal page was read earlier in Stage B and states only that LOC generally does not own rights). The Stage B fallback (Commons 1893 photograph 'at the age of 29', scanned from a 1986 Sri Lankan book, no publication chain) was not used. Retry route (pre-1931 printed portrait with caption): Barrows's The World's Parliament of Religions, vol. 2 (Chicago, 1893). OCR text shows the caption 'H. DHARMAPALA, CEYLON.' under his quotation and the same name in the list of illustrations (p. 861); the page was rendered from the Internet Archive PDF (page scan 2522 x 4152) and the plate cropped. The OCR of Neely's History of the Parliament of Religions (1893) shows a line 'H. DHARMAPALA, Ceylon.' before p. 405 (probably a portrait caption, not opened as an image and not needed). RIGHTS: first published in the United States in 1893, so public domain by age; Internet Archive item record (IA metadata API) states possible-copyright-status NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT, contributor Robarts - University of Toronto, no rights or licence statement; the IA terms page is script-rendered and could not be read, but IA is not a rights holder here. The photograph carries a printed 'Copyright 1893 by' notice (rest not legible); other plates in the volume say 'Copyright, 1893, by J. H. B.', i.e. Barrows, who died in 1902; US copyright on a work published in 1893 expired long ago. CAVEATS: the photographer is unknown; it is a halftone reproduction, not a print from the negative; no separate holder record exists, and identity rests on the printed caption plus the list of illustrations, which is strong because the book is a contemporary record of the Parliament in which he spoke as the Ceylon delegate. KIND likeness (a lifetime photograph, reproduced). PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE (2026-11-23, Wikidata API) Q3518574 label 'Anagarika Dharmapala', description 'Sri Lankan Buddhist revivalist and writer (1864-1933)', no Korean label, born 1864-09-17, died 1933-04-29, human; no candidate file or QID collision found for this slug. REGION south_asia (Sri Lankan; precedent Vivekananda and Kartini). ERA 20th_century (activity 1891-1933). Nationality LK. SENSITIVITY: he is a contested figure (hero of Buddhist revival, and accused by critics of anti-Hindu, anti-Christian and anti-minority rhetoric that fed Sinhala nationalism). The profile scores documented acts only (founding, campaigning, litigating, quarrels, travelling, fundraising, renunciant way of life) and never his beliefs, nationalism or the justice of his cause; rhetoric is recorded in source titles and in dual-edged impact tags, and not scored as a trait. Primary identity is Buddhist religious leader and organiser, not politician; he declined party politics. KOREAN NAME: no Korean Wikipedia article and no Wikidata ko label; the form 아나가리카 다르마팔라 follows NIKL transliteration and recurs in Korean Wikipedia articles on the Buddhism of India, the history of Sri Lanka and religion in India; class transliteration, flagged. ATTRIBUTION: attributable (diaries, notebooks, dated institutions, a court judgment, a contemporaneous 1893 record), with interpretations contested. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Bond, 'Anagarika Dharmapala', Encyclopedia of Buddhism. READ (7 sources besides Wikidata): Bond entry; the Gale student profile; Hewage (St Andrews Encyclopaedia of Theology, full); Sarao chapter (Springer, full text); the Colombo CCIS commemorative volume (chronology, Kemper review and the Maha Bodhi history read; the other essays searched); Barrows vol. 2 (all passages naming him). NOT OPENED: Kemper's Rescued from the Nation, Amunugama's The Lion's Roar, Obeyesekere, Roberts, Seneviratne, Kinnard, Trevithick (all cited secondhand), the BPS Sangharakshita biography (page returned only a redirect), the Calcutta High Court judgment itself, Dharmapala's diaries. INDEPENDENT BEHAVIOURAL FAMILIES: four (the Maha Bodhi Society's own chronology; diary-based scholarship following Kemper; the critical archive-based chapter citing the 1895 judgment; Barrows's contemporary 1893 record, only for 1893). CONTRADICTIONS: birth day (9 or 17 September), where Foster/Blavatsky fit, 1915-20 internment length (one essay says seven years), whether he left the Theosophical Society (Society chronology) or stayed loyal to theosophy to his death (Kemper); none carded as fact beyond what is stated. Not scored: nationalism, political stance, attitudes to Hindus, Christians and Muslims, his physical disability, family relations, diaries' sexual content. MAJOR ACHIEVEMENT GATE: PASS (Maha Bodhi Society and the Bodh Gaya campaign; the 1893 Parliament and global missions; schools, press, Vihara building). SELF-CALIBRATION: concentration lowered proactive_agency (82/0.66 to 78/0.62), persistence (78/0.6 to 74/0.56), conflict_tolerance (78/0.6 to 76/0.58), leadership_drive (76/0.6 to 72/0.56) and autonomy_need (72/0.52 strong inference to 68/0.48 inference); self-calibration lowered persuasiveness (70/0.54 strong inference to 64/0.46 inference), impact_motivation (74/0.56 to 68/0.5), discipline (68/0.5 strong inference to 62/0.44 inference), curiosity (62/0.44 to 58/0.4), resourcefulness (64/0.44 to 58/0.4) and the adaptability evidence type (strong inference to inference at 62/0.46); no row raised.
